title: Normalizing a Table
summary: Split repeated data into its own table and connect it back with a foreign key.
intro: A table that repeats the same facts in many rows is easy to start with and hard to keep correct. In this lesson you split the repeats into their own table, link them back with a foreign key, and rebuild the original rows with a join.
setup:
CREATE TABLE orders_flat (
    id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name text,
    customer_email text,
    item text,
    qty integer
);

INSERT INTO orders_flat (customer_name, customer_email, item, qty) VALUES
    ('Ana Lopez', 'ana@example.com', 'Notebook', 2),
    ('Ben Okafor', 'ben@example.com', 'Pen', 10),
    ('Ana Lopez', 'ana@example.com', 'Pen', 5),
    ('Carla Diaz', 'carla@example.com', 'Stapler', 1),
    ('Ben Okafor', 'ben@example.com', 'Notebook', 3),
    ('Carla Diaz', 'carla@example.com', 'Pen', 4);

steps.title: Spotting and pulling out repeated data
steps.body:
This lesson starts from one wide table, `orders_flat`, where every order carries a full copy of its customer:

```text
 id | customer_name |  customer_email   |   item   | qty
----+---------------+-------------------+----------+-----
  1 | Ana Lopez     | ana@example.com   | Notebook |   2
  2 | Ben Okafor    | ben@example.com   | Pen      |  10
  3 | Ana Lopez     | ana@example.com   | Pen      |   5
  4 | Carla Diaz    | carla@example.com | Stapler  |   1
  5 | Ben Okafor    | ben@example.com   | Notebook |   3
  6 | Carla Diaz    | carla@example.com | Pen      |   4
(6 rows)
```

Each customer's name and email appear twice, and copies drift. Change Ana's email in one row but not the other, and the table now holds two Anas:

```sql
UPDATE orders_flat SET customer_email = 'ana.lopez@example.com' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT DISTINCT customer_name, customer_email FROM orders_flat ORDER BY customer_name, customer_email;
```

```text
 customer_name |    customer_email
---------------+-----------------------
 Ana Lopez     | ana.lopez@example.com
 Ana Lopez     | ana@example.com
 Ben Okafor    | ben@example.com
 Carla Diaz    | carla@example.com
(4 rows)
```

Normalizing fixes this. In plain words, the normal forms ask for:

- **One value per cell.** No lists like `'Pen, Notebook'` in one column.
- **Every column about the whole key, and nothing else.** `qty` is a fact about the order. `customer_email` is a fact about the customer, so it belongs in a customers table.

The first move is to create that table and fill it with one row per distinct customer. `INSERT ... SELECT DISTINCT` copies each pair once:

```sql harness
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name text,
    email text UNIQUE
);
{{code}}
SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY id;
```

```sql
INSERT INTO customers (name, email)
SELECT DISTINCT customer_name, customer_email
FROM orders_flat
ORDER BY customer_email;
```

The `ORDER BY` makes the new ids predictable. Watch for near duplicates: `'Ana@example.com'` and `'ana@example.com'` are distinct values, so clean them with `lower()` and `trim()` first. And if one email appears with two spellings of a name, `DISTINCT` keeps both rows and the `UNIQUE` email rejects the insert, so fix the copies before you split them.

example.title: A customers table
example.prompt: Create a customers table and fill it with one row per distinct customer from orders_flat.
example.output:
CREATE TABLE

INSERT 0 3

 id |    name    |       email
----+------------+-------------------
  1 | Ana Lopez  | ana@example.com
  2 | Ben Okafor | ben@example.com
  3 | Carla Diaz | carla@example.com
(3 rows)
example.explanation: `SELECT DISTINCT` turns six order rows into three customer pairs. `INSERT ... SELECT` writes them into `customers`, and the identity column numbers them in `ORDER BY customer_email` order, so Ana gets id 1. `UNIQUE` on `email` stops the same customer from being added twice later.

steps.title: Connecting it back
steps.body:
`orders_flat` still holds the customer's name and email in every row. Now point each order at its customer instead, in four moves.

1. Add a foreign key column. It starts as `NULL` in every row.
2. Fill it with `UPDATE ... FROM`, matching on a column that is unique in the new table, here the email. If two rows matched, the update would pick one unpredictably.
3. Drop the copied columns. One `ALTER TABLE` can drop several.
4. Join to get the original rows back. If you read that wide shape often, save the join with `CREATE VIEW`.

```sql harness
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name text,
    email text UNIQUE
);
INSERT INTO customers (name, email)
SELECT DISTINCT customer_name, customer_email
FROM orders_flat
ORDER BY customer_email;
{{code}}
SELECT id, customer_name, customer_email, customer_id FROM orders_flat ORDER BY id;
```

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders_flat ADD COLUMN customer_id integer REFERENCES customers (id);

UPDATE orders_flat AS o
SET customer_id = c.id
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.email = o.customer_email;
```

Before you drop anything, check that no row was missed: `SELECT count(*) FROM orders_flat WHERE customer_id IS NULL;` should give 0. `ALTER TABLE orders_flat ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET NOT NULL;` makes the same check for you, fails if a row was missed, and keeps every future order linked. A dropped column is gone for good, so on real data run the whole change inside `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` and roll back if a check fails.

Now each customer's email lives in exactly one row. Changing it is one `UPDATE` on `customers`, and every order sees the new value through the join.

example.title: Orders point at customers
example.prompt: Replace the customer name and email in orders_flat with a customer_id, then rebuild the original rows with a join.
example.code:
-- The customers table from the previous part
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name text,
    email text UNIQUE
);

INSERT INTO customers (name, email)
SELECT DISTINCT customer_name, customer_email
FROM orders_flat
ORDER BY customer_email;

-- 1. A column that points at a customer
ALTER TABLE orders_flat ADD COLUMN customer_id integer REFERENCES customers (id);

-- 2. Fill it by matching on email
UPDATE orders_flat AS o
SET customer_id = c.id
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.email = o.customer_email;

-- 3. Drop the copies
ALTER TABLE orders_flat DROP COLUMN customer_name, DROP COLUMN customer_email;

-- 4. A join rebuilds the old rows
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer_name, c.email AS customer_email, o.item, o.qty
FROM orders_flat AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.id;

After the copies are dropped, the join looks each customer up by id and prints the same rows the flat table held.

Alias the tables as in the example: `i.id` is the value to copy, and an order matches the item whose `name` equals its `item`.
Only one column is copied here, so the drop is `DROP COLUMN item`, and the join selects `i.name AS item`.

recap:
- Repeated copies of the same fact drift out of sync when one copy changes.
- One value per cell, and every column about the whole key and nothing else.
- `INSERT INTO new_table (...) SELECT DISTINCT ...` fills a table with one row per repeated value.
- `ADD COLUMN x_id integer REFERENCES x (id)` adds the link, and `UPDATE ... FROM` fills it by matching a unique column.
- Check for `NULL` links before you `DROP COLUMN` the copies.
- A join gives the original wide rows back whenever you need it, and `CREATE VIEW` can save that join under a name.
